SubTopics: The exigence is the part of a rhetorical situation that inspires, stimulates, provokes, or prompts writers to create a text.
Content: Which of the following best describes the writer's exigence in the passage?

A.Choice: The lack of interest among eligible voters in the political process

B.Choice: The limited resources available to women for changing existing power structures

C.Choice: Widening disparities in the socioeconomic circumstances of American and British women

D.Choice: Public resentment of the high tax rate imposed by the government

SubTopics: Types of evidence may include facts, anecdotes, analogies, statistics, examples, details, illustrations, expert opinions, personal observations, personal experiences, testimonies, or experiments.
Content: In the opening paragraph (lines `1-10`), the writer contrasts a hypothetical rhetorical situation with her own primarily to

A.Choice: illustrate the double standards for men and women in the political realm

B.Choice: explain why women are more reluctant to adopt revolutionary methods than men

C.Choice: emphasize the influence of women on democratic culture in the United States

D.Choice: suggest that American women's civil rights have been eroded in the `text(twentieth)` century

SubTopics: Writers convey their positions through one or more claims that require a defense.
Content: In the second paragraph (lines `11-30`), which of the following best characterizes the writer's position on the relevance of her topic for American women?

A.Choice: Because American women are “so well off” (line `13`), it is unnecessary for them to adopt the methods described by the writer.

B.Choice: Because American women are “so well off” (line `13`), they have access to methods other than those described by the author.

C.Choice: Although the methods described by the writer are best suited for American men, American women could adapt such methods for use in the domestic sphere.

D.Choice: Although American women are perceived as “well off” (line `13`), they should nonetheless consider adopting the methods described by the writer.

SubTopics: Readers infer a writer's tone from the writer's word choice, and especially the positive, negative, or other connotations of those words.
Content: In context, lines `11-23` (“You see ... revolutionary methods”) could be used to support which of the following claims about the writer's tone?

A.Choice: Her tone when discussing American women is patronizing.

B.Choice: Her tone when discussing American men is ingratiating.

C.Choice: She adopts a bold, forthright tone in approaching her subject.

D.Choice: She adopts a reverent, admiring tone in dealing with her subject.

SubTopics: Flaws in a line of reasoning may render an argument specious or illogical.
Content: In the `text(third)` paragraph, the writer criticizes the logic of those who dismiss the methods of British feminists as “irrational” (line `42`) on the grounds that they have

A.Choice: misconstrued the feminists' reasons for employing the strategies they have chosen to employ

B.Choice: overlooked accounts that present a less provocative view of feminist activism in Britain

C.Choice: ignored a key distinction between American feminists and British feminists

D.Choice: assumed that feminists do not understand the normal political process

SubTopics: When developing ideas through cause-effect, writers present a cause, assert effects or consequences of that cause, or present a series of causes and the subsequent effect(s).
Content: In the fourth paragraph (lines `52-67`), the writer introduces a hypothetical scenario primarily to

A.Choice: question the motives of those who demand immediate changes to the status quo

B.Choice: underscore the efficiency of voting as a means of addressing political discontents

C.Choice: spotlight the special political privileges recently accorded to the men of Hartford

D.Choice: encourage women's rights activists to emulate the example of the men of Hartford

SubTopics: The arrangement of clauses, phrases, and words in a sentence can emphasize ideas.
Content: At the end of the passage, the writer uses the “either ... or” construction in lines `75-78` (“they would either ... grievances remedied”) in order to

A.Choice: provide `text(two)` possible explanations for why American women have not yet won the right to vote

B.Choice: offer `text(two)` alternative methods of accomplishing the same goal

C.Choice: assert that patience is critical to smooth political transitions

D.Choice: imply that disruptive action may be the only way of resisting oppression in certain situations

SubTopics: The introduction of an argument introduces the subject and/or writer of the argument to the audience. An introduction may present the argument's thesis. An introduction may orient, engage, and/or focus the audience by presenting quotations, intriguing statements, anecdotes, questions, statistics, data, contextualized information, or a scenario.
Content: Which of the following sentences, if placed before sentence `1`, would both capture the audience's interest and provide the most effective introduction to the topic of the paragraph?

A.Choice: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was launched on `text(December 11, 1998)`, from the Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida.

B.Choice: On `text(September 23, 1999)`, NASA officials were aghast when the `$125` `text(million)` Mars Climate Orbiter vanished as it prepared to enter the red planet's orbit.

C.Choice: As part of a new set of missions intended to survey the planet `text(Mars)`, the Mars Climate Orbiter was launched by NASA scientists to study Mars's climate and weather.

D.Choice: When NASA officials lost contact with their Mars Climate Orbiter on `text(September 23, 1999)`, they immediately instigated a search for the spacecraft using NASA's Deep Space Network of radio antennae.

SubTopics: Transitional elements are words or other elements (phrases, clauses, sentences, or paragraphs) that assist in creating coherence among sentences, paragraphs, or sections in a text by showing relationships among ideas.
Content: In sentence `2` (reproduced below), the writer wants an effective transition from the introductory paragraph to the main idea of the passage.

:ibox:The culprit was a discrepancy in the software that controlled the spacecraft's `ul(text(thrusters: one team of engineers had calculated the force needed from the thrusters in pounds, an imperial unit, while another team calculated the force in newtons, a metric unit))`.
Which of the following versions of the underlined text best achieves this purpose?

B.Choice: thrusters; the data from the spacecraft and the data from NASA's computers on the ground had not been matching up for months since the launch of the Orbiter

C.Choice: thrusters—software that was used to calculate the trajectory the Orbiter needed to take in order to enter Mars's orbit successfully

D.Choice: thrusters: `text(four)` thrusters were used for trajectory correction maneuvers as well as pitch and yaw control, while another `text(four)` were used for roll control

SubTopics: A thesis is the main, overarching claim a writer is seeking to defend or prove by using reasoning supported by evidence.
Content: In sentence `3` (reproduced below), which of the following versions of the underlined text best establishes the writer's position on the main argument of the passage?
:ibox:The Orbiter mission failure is just one reason, albeit an extremely expensive one, that the United States `ul(text(needs to abandon future Mars survey missions))`.

C.Choice: needs to adopt the metric system

D.Choice: should partner with other countries on future missions to outer space

SubTopics: Commentary explains the significance and relevance of evidence in relation to the line of reasoning.
Content: In sentence `9` (reproduced below), the writer wants to provide a convincing explanation for why switching to the metric system would benefit United States industries.

Switching to the metric system would also benefit United States `ul(text(industries; the European Union, for example, has been requiring its member states to standardize their metric systems since 1971))`.

SubTopics: When writers concede, they accept all or a portion of a competing position or claim as correct, agree that the competing position or claim is correct under a different set of circumstances, or acknowledge the limitations of their own argument.
Content: In the `text(fourth)` paragraph (sentences `10-11`), the writer wants to expand on the concession that converting to the metric system may seem difficult. Which of the following claims would best achieve this purpose?

A.Choice: Many attempts to make the United States adopt the metric system have already been made.

B.Choice: The units in the imperial system were `text(first)` officially defined by the Office of the Exchequer in Great Britain in `text(1824)`, but they have existed as the Winchester Standards since `text(1588)`.

C.Choice: Some people in Great Britain, which adopted the metric system `text(decades)` ago, want to return to the imperial system.

D.Choice: It would be extremely costly as well as confusing for the United States to manage the overwhelming task of converting everything from road signs to measuring cups to the metric system.

SubTopics: When writers rebut, they offer a contrasting perspective on an argument and its evidence or provide alternative evidence to propose that all or a portion of a competing position or claim is invalid.
Content: In the `text(fourth)` paragraph (sentences `10-11`), the writer wants to provide further evidence to rebut the claim that converting to the metric system might be difficult. Which of the following pieces of evidence would best achieve this purpose?

B.Choice: An interview from an opponent of adopting the metric system in the United States

C.Choice: A description of the successful adoption of the metric system by Great Britain, which had previously used the imperial system

D.Choice: A United States government report estimating the cost of converting highway signs on state roads at `$334` `text(million dollars)`

Content: As the Internet age changes what and how people read, there has been considerable debate about the future of public libraries. While some commentators question whether libraries can stay relevant, others see new possibilities for libraries in the changing dynamics of today's society.

Carefully read the `text(six)` sources, including the introductory information for each source. Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on the role, if any, that public libraries should serve in the future.
In your response you should do the following:

:ibox:• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Select and use evidence from at least `text(three)` of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning. Indicate clearly the sources used through direct quotation, paraphrase, or summary. Sources may be cited as Source `A`, Source `B`, etc., or by using the description in parentheses.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

In `text(May 2012)` former United States Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who was the first African American woman to hold that position, gave a commencement speech to the graduating class of Southern Methodist University, a private university in Dallas, Texas. The passage above is an excerpt from that speech. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Rice makes to convey her message to her audience.

• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.

In your response you should do the following:
